bib.title: Holding on to your gains by watching for drift (Chapter 12, Machine Learning Engineering in Action)

question: What kinds of drift degrade a production ML model, how are they monitored, and how should a team respond?
hypothesis: Models will drift; there is no static implementation, so every production model needs continuous monitoring and a defined retraining response.
contributions: Six-way taxonomy of drift (feature, label, concept, prediction, reality, feedback) with measurement methods and corrective actions (Table 12.1)

results.claim: Worked example: a temperature unit change (F to C) upstream shifts a feature and collapses revenue lift from positive to a large loss.
results.setup: Fictional ice cream propensity-to-buy model, monthly passive retraining, emails sent at propensity > 60%, no monitoring; mid-June feed change
results.quote: From a revenue lift of 20%, the test group is now showing a 300% loss.

results.claim: Label drift monitoring for classifiers should use Fisher's exact test with a very low alpha.
results.setup: Compare recent prediction class counts in a time window with validation (test) predictions from training
results.quote: Fisher’s exact test with a very low alpha value (< 0.01)

results.claim: Label drift can leave holdout loss equal or better while a fixed send threshold (e.g. 90% probability) admits nearly all customers, inflating cost.
results.setup: Marketing sends customized coupons only above threshold; prediction distribution shifts after eight weeks (Fig 12.2)
results.quote: only if the probability for using one was above 90%?
results.note: Eight weeks appears in the Fig 12.2 labels.

results.claim: Approximate retraining periodicity ranges from hourly/daily (recommendation) to semiannual/annual (equipment failure); fraud is biweekly, churn monthly, image labeling two to six months.
results.setup: Author's experience across industries; row Image content labeling (attribution: % error in classification). Loosely approximated.
results.table: Table 12.2, row Image content labeling, column Retraining periodicity (approximate): Two to six months
results.note: Other rows: churn Monthly; CLV Weekly; Transportation/demand pricing Monthly; recommendation Hourly or daily; fraud Biweekly; equipment failure Semiannually or annually; sales forecasting Daily or weekly. Table layout in extracted text is garbled for row-to-cell mapping.

limits: No empirical data: all examples are fictional ice cream scenarios and the retraining periodicities are the author's loose estimates
No threshold values given for mean/variance/SPC alerts except alpha < 0.01
Drift taxonomy is the author's own and differs from the covariate/prior/concept shift split in the literature (feature drift ~ covariate shift, label drift here means prediction-distribution shift)
No code, no named drift library; only MLflow tracking is mentioned
practices: Monitor every production model for drift; no model is static (p336).
Log training-time feature statistics (mean, median, stddev, IQR) in MLflow so drift checks need no expensive recomputation (p345).
Feature monitoring: compare training-time vs recent mean/median/stddev/IQR and alert when the delta exceeds a level (p345).
Distribution equivalency: convert continuous features to pdf and categoricals to pmf, compare with Wasserstein metric or Hellinger distance (p345).
Apply statistical process control (Western Electric rules) on smoothed feature values, and SPC on categorical membership share (p345).
Label drift for classifiers: store windowed prediction class counts, track label ratios with acceptable deviation, test with Fisher's exact test alpha < 0.01 (p341).
Label drift for regressors: windowed mean, median, stddev, IQR of predictions with thresholds; optionally fit a distribution and compare with Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (p341).

Concept drift: log primary loss and the attribution (business) metric, aggregate prediction statistics over a window, trend them, and treat unexplained drift as grounds to retrain or revisit features (p342-343).
Three simple feature checks: step change in mean, step change in variance (needs longer window to avoid false positives), and spike in variation beyond history (p348-349).

Retrain passively on a schedule (sliding window or all data), comparing prior production and new model on the same fresh holdout; keep the winner; alert when no new model wins for too many iterations (p351-352).
Retrain actively when monitored prediction distributions or attribution leave tolerance or SPC/static thresholds; promote winner via CI/CD (p352).
For obvious ETL faults, repair or rescale features, retrain, validate on new holdout (p350).
If business impact is statistically significantly negative, stop using the model immediately, do root-cause analysis, shut down permanently if the benefit is gone (p350).
For reality drift, either abandon or rebuild after feature engineering; never quietly ignore (p347).
Detect feedback drift by recording metrics at each retraining and watching for failure to return to acceptable loss (p347).
Avoid kitchen-sink feature vectors because they make feature monitoring hard to scale (p337).

terms.definition: Shift in input feature data, e.g. a numeric scaling change from upstream ETL; includes feature ignorance, inference data beyond the training range
Inference data arrives beyond the bounds of what the model was trained on
A shift in the prediction distribution, typically caused by a shift in the distribution of several critical features
Introduction of a large latent (not collected) variable that has a strong influence on a model’s predictions
Affects predictions like label drift but is directly related to a feature that is part of the model; detected through feature monitoring and attribution measurement
A special case of concept drift: foundational, unforeseen outside shifts (pandemic, black swan) with profound large-scale impact
Acting on the model's outputs shrinks variance in the data until little signal remains (diminishing returns)
Scheduled job trains on a sliding window or all data and compares with the production model on new holdout
Automated, triggered retraining when monitored attribution or prediction quality leaves tolerance
